title: Student AI Use Is About Much More Than School Rules
author: Alicia Anderson
source: Thomas B. Fordham Institute, Flypaper (fordhaminstitute.org), September 17, 2026
summary: Alicia Anderson, writing as a parent for the Fordham Institute, situates the current wave of school AI restrictions, including New York City's moratorium on student-facing AI through eighth grade and Los Angeles's total ban, within a broader 'techlash' driven by parents across the political spectrum. She argues that because it took more than a decade to recognize the harms of smartphones, social media, and school-issued devices, schools and families cannot wait as long on AI. Her central claim is that minutes-based screen limits and access rules do not resolve the harder questions AI raises, which are more moral than technical: honesty, judgment, and whether struggling through difficult work has value beyond the finished product. Drawing on a back-to-school conversation with her daughter's humanities teacher, she describes adults torn between preparing children to use AI and evidence that it erodes learning, noting that AI-assisted students can earn better grades without acquiring knowledge. The move of the piece is to place responsibility on parents, working in partnership with educators, to talk with children about when and whether to use AI and to build their capacity to reason and work independently.
points: Anderson argues that screen-time and access limits, though welcome, cannot settle the moral questions AI raises about honesty, effort, and judgment.
She contrasts her oldest child's tech-saturated high school experience with her youngest's elementary teachers, who now ask whether a task works without technology rather than seeking ways to add it.

A recent analysis of closed-book test scores suggests AI-using students gain grades and efficiency without acquiring knowledge, while teacher-generated AI 'slop' undermines the message that effort is central to learning.
Perceived peer use turns each assignment into a moral reckoning for students who would prefer to avoid AI, a burden few kids are equipped to handle when adults lack shared norms.
Her prescription is for parents to ask about AI use, know school policies, stress the limits of shortcuts, and partner with teachers, treating a pause on school AI as necessary but insufficient.
quotes: It took well over a decade to see the alarming impact of smartphones, social media, and school-issued devices on children, and longer still to demand action to protect students from harmful effects. We clearly can’t wait that long on AI.

In addition to increasingly clear impacts on learning, AI use raises complex questions about honesty, judgment, and whether struggling through difficult work has inherent value separate from the final product. Parents who believe a child’s moral education starts at home need to engage in conversations about when and how—or if—the technology should be used.

For my youngest child, in her last year of elementary school, teachers seem noticeably more cautious about technology in their classrooms. Instead of seeking out ways to incorporate tech, they ask whether the task works without it.

Action on screen time, driven by consensus, is a welcome development. Yet limiting the number of minutes a child spends on their school-issued device does not resolve the difficult questions—more moral than technical—that come with an AI future.
Students may earn better grades for less work, but a recent analysis of closed-book test scores confirms that students using AI are not obtaining knowledge along the way.
And even if kids want to avoid AI, their perceptions of peer use mean that every assignment brings a moral reckoning over whether the cost to not use AI is too high.

Pressing “pause” on AI in schools is necessary but insufficient. Today’s students will not know a world without this new technology, and it’s up to the adults in their lives to equip them with the human capacity to debate and decide how it should be used.
